checkpoints: "Faster" describes a query shape running on a storage model, not the database itself.
The real question is: what is the system's dominant query — point lookup by key, range/sort, indexed filter, reading a whole aggregate, or a many-to-many relation — and what consistency does it need?
SQL's tables plus B-tree indexes make range and indexed filter cheap.
JOIN lets you normalize the schema to avoid duplicated data.
A document store makes point-lookup-by-id and reading a whole aggregate cheap because no JOIN is needed, at the cost of expensive cross-document filters or many-to-many relations.

On consistency, SQL leans toward ACID/strong consistency (money, inventory), while many NoSQL systems lean toward availability + eventual consistency to make horizontal scaling easier — this is exactly the CAP trade-off surfacing at the engine-choice step.
There is no "best" engine, only the one that best matches the dominant query shape plus the consistency requirement.
The way to confirm it is benchmarking the same dataset, not guessing.
An index is a pre-sorted auxiliary data structure (commonly a B-tree of sorted keys in RDBMSs) that lets the database locate needed rows without scanning the whole table.
This changes the cost profile from O(n) for a sequential scan to roughly O(log n) for an index lookup.
Concretely, for 100,000 rows that's about 17 steps versus a full scan of 100,000.
The advantage isn't fixed — it widens further as the table grows larger.
On a small table the query planner may still choose a sequential scan because it's actually cheaper there.
Indexes are not a free win — they're a trade-off: every write must update each relevant index (slowing writes), and every index also consumes extra storage (bloating disk usage).
The rule of thumb is to index only queries that are genuinely hot/frequent reads.
Always verify the need and benefit with a real measurement (e.g., EXPLAIN ANALYZE) rather than adding indexes on a hunch.

A RANGE shard key on a monotonically increasing field like `createdAt` routes every freshly-inserted document into the same last chunk, so one shard absorbs essentially all new-write traffic while the other shards sit idle — the opposite of what sharding is meant to achieve.

The balancer can rebalance existing chunks across shards, but it cannot fix a key that keeps generating new documents at one end of the range — the imbalance regenerates continuously as long as the shard key stays monotonic, so this is a design flaw, not a transient condition.

`updateMany({ tier: 'free' }, ...)` filters on a field the router has no chunk map for, so mongos cannot resolve a single target shard and instead broadcasts the write to every shard, each one taking locks while scanning its own slice for matches — a scatter-gather write that grows more expensive and lock-heavy as the cluster grows.

Neither the hot-shard skew nor the broadcast write shows up as a failure in CI, a clean migration run, or an error-free cron execution, because both problems only manifest under real write volume and cluster size rather than through functional correctness.

The shard-key fix is to reshard onto a hashed key (e.g. hashed `userId`) or a compound key led by a high-cardinality, non-monotonic field, so newly-inserted documents spread evenly across chunks instead of concentrating on one.

Resharding a live collection is expensive and hard to reverse, which is why the shard-key choice is the review blocker, whereas the maintenance job's untargeted filter is a comparatively cheap, low-risk change to fix later.

A tier-wide `updateMany` that intentionally touches documents across all shards is an acceptable broadcast as long as the review explicitly calls it out as deliberate; the actual risk is an unintentional broadcast on what should have been a targeted, single-shard write. Point-write queries elsewhere in the codebase, such as `updateOne({ userId, ... }, ...)`, should always include the shard key in their filter so the router can target a single shard.

Verifying the fix means seeding data through the new shard key and checking document/chunk distribution across shards — counts should land roughly even instead of skewed toward the newest chunk — and running `.explain()` on the maintenance query to confirm it resolves to `SINGLE_SHARD` rather than `SHARD_MERGE` once it's meant to be targeted.

A leading wildcard in a pattern match — `LIKE '%keyword%'` in SQL or a Mongoose `$regex` with no anchored start — removes any fixed prefix for an index to seek from, so neither PostgreSQL's B-tree on `name` nor MongoDB's default index can be used, and both engines fall back to scanning every row or document.

Because the fallback scan touches the entire table or collection on every call, latency rises linearly with row count: a search that feels instant at a few hundred rows becomes slow at hundreds of thousands, and the query plan confirms it — `Seq Scan` with a large `Rows Removed by Filter` on Postgres, `COLLSCAN` with `totalDocsExamined` near the full collection size on MongoDB.

A plain B-tree index on `name` only speeds up patterns with a fixed, known prefix, such as `LIKE 'keyword%'` or exact equality, because a B-tree can only jump to where that prefix starts in sorted order; it cannot help a leading-wildcard search, so adding one adds write cost to every insert and update while giving no read benefit for this query shape.

The actual fix is to reach for a structure purpose-built for tokenized substring or relevance search rather than a generic index: PostgreSQL's native full-text search (`tsvector` plus a GIN index), the `pg_trgm` extension for trigram-based substring matching, or an external engine like Elasticsearch when ranking, fuzzy matching, or faceting is also needed.

Bringing in a dedicated search engine turns it into a secondary store that must be kept in sync with the primary database — via CDC, an outbox pattern, or a reindex job — which adds an operational moving part and eventual-consistency risk, a cost worth paying only when text search is a genuine hot path rather than a rarely used admin filter.
Verifying the fix means re-running the search at a realistic catalog size (hundreds of thousands of rows) and confirming that latency no longer grows linearly with the number of rows.

Latency improving is not sufficient proof by itself — the query plan should be re-checked after the fix, expecting `Index Scan`/`Bitmap Index Scan` on the GIN or trigram index in Postgres, or `IXSCAN` on MongoDB's text index, to confirm the full scan is actually gone rather than just coincidentally faster.

A slow reporting query against a large unpartitioned table often bundles two independent costs together: how much data the query has to scan, and which database node absorbs the load while running it — treating them as one problem hides that they need two separate fixes.

Running a read-only report through the primary connection means it competes with live writes for the same CPU and I/O capacity, even though nothing about a report requires it to touch the primary at all.

Range-partitioning a table like `orders` by `created_at` lets the query planner prune to only the partition(s) overlapping the requested date range instead of scanning the whole table, cutting rows scanned by orders of magnitude for date-filtered queries.
Partitioning by the same column a report already filters on (`created_at`) turns a full-table scan into a scan of one narrow slice of data, which is the core mechanism behind the speedup.
Once data is partitioned by date, retiring old data becomes a fast `DROP PARTITION` instead of a slow, lock-heavy `DELETE` over millions of rows.

Routing a read-only report to a replica connection instead of the primary removes its contention with live writes, at the cost of the report seeing data that is only eventually consistent due to replication lag — acceptable for a monthly aggregate but not for anything requiring real-time accuracy.

Partitioning only helps if the partitions actually exist ahead of the incoming data and are keyed correctly; rows that don't match any defined partition fall into a default/catch-all partition, which silently loses pruning and can quietly degrade performance again.

Confirming the fix worked requires evidence, not assumption: running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` should show only the target partition being scanned, and re-measuring report latency and primary CPU before and after should show the primary is no longer impacted by the report's read load.
Centralize the read/write split behind one small routing contract so business code never picks a node (primary vs replica) by hand.
This builds on the existing createQueryRunner("master")/("slave") pattern, just raised one level into an explicit interface.
Default rule enforced in exactly one place: every write (and any read that must see its own just-written data) routes to the primary; every ordinary read routes to a replica.

An explicit escape hatch lets a caller request a strong/primary read (e.g. find(id, { consistency: 'strong' }) or a dedicated findStrong()) for a sensitive read-after-write path, keeping the fast replica default for everything else as a deliberate choice.

Justification: routing is a property of the operation — write vs. read, and how strong a consistency the read needs — not a property of the caller, so hiding master/slave selection behind one interface lets the underlying topology change without touching business call sites.

The trade-off is defended openly: replica reads are eventually consistent (bounded by whatever replication lag currently measures), so read-your-writes is an escape hatch, not the default — overusing it for every read defeats the point of read-scaling by dumping load back onto the primary.

The contract must also define failure/extension behavior: a load-balancing/selection policy across multiple replicas (e.g. round-robin), and a decision for when the only replica is unreachable or lag crosses a threshold — fail over to the primary automatically or surface the staleness, never silently serve stale data on a path that matters.

Centralize the store choice behind one storage-routing point (a small registry/factory keyed by entity), deciding based on dominant query shape and consistency need, so no service picks its own client (TypeORM vs Mongoose).
Orders and payments are JOIN-heavy, need range queries, and can't tolerate a wrong balance — so they're ACID and land in PostgreSQL.
The catalog is mostly point-lookup/whole-aggregate reads with a volatile, fast-changing shape — so it scales fine on MongoDB.

Against "one generic repository interface both engines implement transparently": that hides a lie, not just an implementation detail — a caller assuming every repository gives ACID/JOIN semantics will eventually break against the Mongo-backed one, and forcing Mongo to fake a JOIN or forcing Postgres to fake a schema-less whole-aggregate read throws away the exact strength each engine was chosen for.

The contract should surface which guarantees a given repository offers (transactional? point-lookup only? cross-entity JOIN?) rather than paper over the difference with one interface that quietly lies to half its callers.

Any new entity must explicitly declare its store in the registry — ideally enforced by a lint/CI check that fails if it doesn't — instead of silently defaulting to whichever client happens to be imported.

A query that genuinely needs both orders and catalog data together must be composed explicitly at the application layer (two calls joined in code), never hidden behind the boundary as if it were one native query.
This only pays off when the query-shape benefit is real — for a small system, one well-chosen engine beats operating and syncing two stores just because a diagram looked neat.
Scaling up (vertically) buys time but hits a ceiling and leaves a single point of failure.
The architecturally correct fix is a read/write split, where the primary is the sole write node.
The primary writes its changes to the WAL and streams them to a read-only replica.
The application routes writes to the primary and reads to the replica.
Because reads dominate 50:1, offloading them to the replica lifts read throughput almost linearly while the primary focuses purely on writes.
Crucially this does NOT solve write scaling — there is still exactly one primary — so a write-heavy problem needs sharding instead of replication.
The accepted cost is asynchronous replication lag: reads through the replica can be momentarily stale relative to what was just written.
The router computes rather than searches: it derives the target shard from the shard key via the config server's chunk map.
findByUserId filters on the shard key, so the router hashes it, knows the one shard the chunk lives on, and sends a targeted single-shard query with minimal docs examined.
findByCountry filters on an ordinary field the router cannot map to a shard, so it broadcasts the query to every shard and merges the results.
With N shards that broadcast-and-merge means N round-trips per query, which is why performance degrades further as more shards are added.
The design consequence is that hot query paths must be built around the shard key.
For an unavoidable off-key hot query, add a secondary index or a dedicated search store.
Remember that a secondary index only accelerates the per-shard scan and never removes the fan-out across shards.

Correctness under concurrency must dominate raw latency for money and stock — reading a stale balance or double-decrementing inventory is a bug users and finance will both notice, not just a slow response.
ACID's atomicity and isolation guarantee that inside one transaction, a multi-table JOIN still sees one consistent snapshot.
ACID also guarantees write-safety: two concurrent writers can't both "win" on the same row.

Document stores deliberately trade toward availability and horizontal scale — a read can legitimately see a value that hasn't finished replicating yet, which is a CAP-theorem trade-off, not a defect, so a NoSQL benchmark winning on some read query doesn't contradict the SQL choice.
The precise line for accepting eventual consistency is the data's tolerance to delay: a product catalog, application logs, or an activity feed can serve a slightly stale read with no real damage.

The mature design is polyglot persistence — keep the transactional core (orders, payments, inventory) on a strongly-consistent SQL engine and only push delay-tolerant data to NoSQL, because speed on the wrong answer is meaningless.
